body:
Nature of seismic waves

When energy is suddenly released within the Earth, it travels through surrounding materials in the form of seismic waves. The scientific study of earthquakes and seismic waves is called seismology.

A seismograph is an instrument used to record ground vibrations. The resulting record is called a seismogram.

Seismic waves are broadly divided into body waves and surface waves.

Body waves

Body waves travel through the Earth's interior. They are classified into primary waves and secondary waves.

Primary waves (P-waves)

P-waves are longitudinal or compressional waves. Particles of the material vibrate parallel to the direction in which the wave travels, producing alternating compression and expansion.

P-waves are the fastest seismic waves and therefore generally reach a recording station first. They can travel through solids, liquids and gases.

Secondary waves (S-waves)

S-waves are transverse or shear waves. Particles vibrate perpendicular to the direction of wave propagation.

S-waves travel more slowly than P-waves. They require a material capable of resisting shear deformation and therefore cannot propagate as shear waves through liquids or gases.

The passage of S-waves through the mantle demonstrates that most mantle material is solid.

Surface waves

Surface waves travel predominantly along or near the Earth's surface. They generally arrive after body waves and often cause the strongest damaging ground movements.

Two important types are:

  • Love waves: Produce horizontal, side-to-side shear motion.
  • Rayleigh waves: Produce a rolling motion involving both vertical and horizontal ground displacement.

Surface waves are important for understanding earthquake damage, while body waves are particularly useful for investigating the Earth's deep interior.

Changes in seismic wave behaviour

Seismic wave speeds depend on the density and elastic properties of the material through which they travel. A change in rock composition, physical state or rigidity can change their speed and direction.

When waves encounter an internal boundary, they may be reflected or refracted. Scientists study these changes to identify internal discontinuities.

At the boundary between the solid mantle and liquid outer core, P-waves undergo a sharp reduction in speed and substantial refraction, while directly travelling S-waves cannot pass through the liquid.

Seismic shadow zones

A seismic shadow zone is a region on the Earth's surface where particular directly arriving seismic waves from an earthquake are not recorded.

The position of a shadow zone is expressed as the angular distance from the earthquake's epicentre, measured around the Earth.

WaveApproximate shadow zoneMain reason
P-wave105°–145°Strong refraction at the liquid core
S-waveBeyond 105° up to 180°Cannot travel directly through the liquid outer core

The angular limits are rounded school-level values. Exact boundaries can differ slightly according to the seismic model and type of arrival being considered.

P-waves can travel through the liquid outer core and reach recording stations beyond their shadow zone. Direct S-waves do not reappear in the same way because the liquid outer core cannot transmit shear waves.

Secondary waves produced through conversion between seismic wave types may still be detected in regions described as shadow zones. The basic classification concerns direct seismic arrivals.

Discovering the structure of the core

Seismic observations established the existence of a core that behaves differently from the overlying mantle. The disappearance of direct S-waves and the refraction of P-waves demonstrate that the outer core is liquid.

Further analysis of seismic arrivals established the existence of a distinct inner core. In 1936, Danish seismologist Inge Lehmann identified evidence for the inner core through the behaviour of P-waves. Subsequent seismic investigations established its solid nature.

Prelims focus

  • P-waves are longitudinal, faster and capable of travelling through solids and fluids.
  • S-waves are transverse and cannot travel through liquids.
  • Love waves produce horizontal shear; Rayleigh waves produce rolling ground motion.
  • The conventional P-wave shadow zone extends from approximately 105° to 145°.
  • The direct S-wave shadow zone extends beyond approximately 105°.
  • Trap: The absence of direct S-waves through the core establishes the liquid nature of the outer core, not the entire core.

[References: NCERT, Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Class 11, 2025–26, Chapter 3, pp. 19–23, Figures 3.1–3.2; Gujarat State Board of School Textbooks, Geography, Class 11, 2020 reprint, Chapter 4, pp. 22–25; USGS, The Interior of the Earth; USGS, Are the Tectonic Plates Floating on Magma?; USGS, Earthquake Animations, Seismic Shadow Zone. Online sources consulted 27 November 2026.]

title: Seismic Waves and the Evidence for a Liquid Outer Core

body:
The continental drift hypothesis

The present arrangement of continents and oceans is the result of geological changes extending over hundreds of millions of years. Continents have repeatedly changed their positions relative to one another.

In 1912, German meteorologist Alfred Wegener presented a comprehensive hypothesis of continental drift. He proposed that continents now separated by oceans had once been joined together.

Wegener called the ancient supercontinent Pangaea, meaning all land, and the vast surrounding ocean Panthalassa, meaning all sea.

Pangaea began to break apart approximately 200 million years ago. In the simplified reconstruction, it separated into 2 large continental masses:

  • Laurasia: The northern continental mass, associated broadly with North America and much of Eurasia.
  • Gondwanaland: The southern continental mass, including the ancestral landmasses of South America, Africa, India, Antarctica and Australia.

The subsequent fragmentation and movement of these continental masses contributed to the formation of the present continents and ocean basins.

Evidence supporting continental drift

Matching continental margins

The eastern margin of South America and the western margin of Africa fit together remarkably well. Their resemblance becomes clearer when the submerged continental margins are considered instead of relying only on present coastlines, which have been modified by erosion, deposition and sea-level changes.

Similar rocks across oceans

Ancient rock formations on the Brazilian coast have geological similarities with rocks in western Africa. Comparable rocks of approximately 2,000 million years in age occur on opposite sides of the Atlantic Ocean.

Such geological similarities are consistent with the former connection of these continental regions.

Distribution of fossils

Similar fossils occur in continental regions that are now separated by vast oceans. Their distribution is difficult to explain if the continents always occupied their present positions.

  • Mesosaurus: Fossils of this small aquatic reptile have been found in South America and southern Africa. Its restricted aquatic habitat makes dispersal across a vast open ocean an unlikely explanation.
  • Glossopteris: Fossils of this extinct seed-fern occur across several former Gondwana landmasses, including India, South America, Africa, Antarctica and Australia.

Ancient glacial deposits

A tillite is a sedimentary rock formed from consolidated glacial deposits.

Comparable ancient glacial deposits occur in India and other former Gondwana regions. Their distribution becomes easier to explain when these landmasses are reconstructed as parts of a common southern continent that experienced extensive glaciation.

This evidence also demonstrates that a region's ancient climate may have differed significantly from its present climate because the landmass occupied a different geographical position.

Historical argument from placer deposits

Placer deposits are concentrations of valuable minerals formed through natural processes such as the transport and sorting of sediments.

Wegener's continental-drift arguments included a proposed relationship between gold-bearing rocks in Brazil and placer gold deposits along the coast of Ghana. This is a traditional historical argument rather than a conclusive modern demonstration that Ghana's gold deposits originated in Brazil.

Limitations of the original hypothesis

Wegener suggested that forces associated with the Earth's rotation and tidal attraction could explain continental movement. However, these proposed forces were inadequate to move continents through the surrounding oceanic material as his original hypothesis required.

The hypothesis also lacked a satisfactory explanation of how the ocean floor behaved during continental movement.

Later investigations of the ocean floor, magnetic reversals and mantle processes provided the missing evidence. They led to the modern theory of plate tectonics, which explains the movement of both continental and oceanic lithosphere.

What actually moves?

Continents do change their positions, as Wegener proposed. In modern plate tectonics, however, continents move as parts of lithospheric plates rather than independently ploughing through stationary oceanic crust.

Prelims focus

  • Alfred Wegener proposed continental drift in 1912.
  • Pangaea was the supercontinent; Panthalassa was the surrounding ocean.
  • India formed part of Gondwanaland.
  • Mesosaurus fossils connect South America and southern Africa.
  • Tillites indicate ancient glaciation and support continental reconstruction.
  • Trap: Wegener's proposed driving forces are not the accepted mechanism of modern plate tectonics.

[References: NCERT, Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Class 11, 2025–26, Chapter 4, pp. 27–29; Gujarat State Board of School Textbooks, Geography, Class 11, 2020 reprint, Chapter 5, Continents and Oceans; USGS, This Dynamic Earth, Historical Perspective and Developing the Theory. Online sources consulted 27 November 2026.]

title: Continental Drift and the Evidence for Moving Continents

body:
Relief of the ocean floor

The ocean floor is not a uniform, flat surface. It contains extensive mountain chains, deep trenches and broad basins. The discovery and investigation of these features helped explain how the Earth's surface changes.

Two important ocean-floor features are closely related to tectonic activity:

  • Mid-oceanic ridges: Long submarine mountain systems associated with the separation of tectonic plates and the generation of oceanic crust.
  • Oceanic trenches: Deep, elongated depressions commonly formed where one oceanic plate bends and descends beneath another plate.

The sea-floor spreading hypothesis

Harry Hess developed the hypothesis of sea-floor spreading in the early 1960s and published his influential account in 1962.

According to this hypothesis, new oceanic crust forms along mid-oceanic ridges and gradually moves away from them on both sides. Older oceanic lithosphere may eventually descend into the mantle at subduction zones.

How new oceanic crust forms

  1. Adjacent tectonic plates move apart along a divergent boundary.
  2. Hot mantle material rises beneath the separating plates.
  3. The reduction in pressure causes some mantle rock to melt, generating magma.
  4. Basaltic magma rises, cools and solidifies, producing new oceanic crust.
  5. Continued plate separation carries the previously formed crust away from the ridge.

As oceanic lithosphere moves away from the spreading centre, it cools, becomes thicker and generally increases in density. Old, dense oceanic lithosphere can eventually descend into the mantle at convergent boundaries.

Evidence for sea-floor spreading

Age of ocean-floor rocks

Oceanic rocks near the crest of a mid-oceanic ridge are generally younger than those farther away. The progressive increase in age away from spreading centres demonstrates that new crust forms at the ridges.

The ocean floor is generally geologically younger than the oldest continental rocks because oceanic lithosphere is repeatedly created and recycled.

Magnetic stripes and polarity reversals

The Earth's magnetic field has reversed its polarity many times during geological history.

As basaltic lava cools and solidifies, its magnetic minerals preserve information about the direction of the Earth's magnetic field at that time.

Continuous production of oceanic crust during successive periods of normal and reversed magnetic polarity creates bands of differently magnetised rocks on the ocean floor.

These magnetic bands occur in approximately matching patterns on opposite sides of spreading ridges. Their symmetry indicates that new crust forms near the ridge and moves outward on both sides.

Ocean-floor sediments

Sediments are generally thinner near newly formed oceanic crust and become thicker over older portions of the ocean floor because older surfaces have had more time to accumulate deposits. Local sediment supply can modify this general pattern.

Volcanic and earthquake activity

Mid-oceanic ridges are associated with volcanic activity, high heat flow and shallow earthquakes. Oceanic trenches and adjacent subduction zones are associated with earthquakes occurring at a wider range of depths.

These patterns support the formation of oceanic crust at spreading centres and the recycling of oceanic lithosphere at convergent boundaries.

Why the Earth does not continually expand

The formation of new oceanic crust does not imply that the Earth must continuously increase in size. Oceanic lithosphere is also consumed through subduction, in which a plate descends beneath another plate and returns material to the mantle.

Sea-floor spreading and subduction are complementary geological processes. They explain the renewal of the ocean floor and the changing dimensions of ocean basins.

Prelims focus

  • Harry Hess is associated with the sea-floor spreading hypothesis.
  • New oceanic crust forms at mid-oceanic ridges.
  • Ocean-floor rocks generally become older away from a spreading ridge.
  • Approximately symmetrical magnetic stripes record successive polarity reversals.
  • Subduction recycles older oceanic lithosphere into the mantle.
  • Trap: Mid-oceanic ridges are primarily sites of crustal creation, whereas oceanic trenches commonly occur at sites of subduction.

[References: NCERT, Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Class 11, 2025–26, Chapter 4, pp. 29–32; USGS, This Dynamic Earth, Developing the Theory and Harry Hammond Hess; Smithsonian Ocean, How the Ocean Floor Helped Seal the Deal for Plate Tectonics. Online sources consulted 27 November 2026.]
